title: Tax planning for company directors before 5 April 2027
description: Salary vs dividends for 2026/27, your basic-rate band, pensions, the £100k trap and the EV deadline: what directors can do before 5 April 2027.
author: Barry Adams
why: Directors start thinking about year-end planning after the Budget and before April. This gives Ltd Premium and Tax Boost prospects a clear reason to book a planning meeting before 5 April 2027.

html:
If you run your own limited company, the next few months are your last chance to shape your 2026/27 tax bill. Before 5 April 2027, check your salary and dividend mix, use any spare basic-rate band, consider an employer pension contribution, and watch the £100,000 line. If an electric company car is on your list, the 100% write-off ends on 31 March 2027.

This is general information. The right mix depends on your own numbers, so treat it as a list of things to look at, not a plan.

The 2026/27 numbers you're working with

The 28 October 2026 Budget didn't change any of these for 2026/27, and HMRC's Budget rates table keeps dividend rates the same for 2027/28 too.

2026/27Figure
Personal allowance£12,570
Basic rate band ends at£50,270 of total income
Employee National Insurance starts (primary threshold)£12,570
Employer National Insurance starts (secondary threshold)£5,000, at 15%
Dividend allowance£500
Dividend tax rates10.75% basic, 35.75% higher, 39.35% additional
Corporation Tax19% on profits up to £50,000, 25% over £250,000, marginal relief in between
Employment Allowance£10,500

One thing to note: the basic and higher dividend rates went up by two points in April 2026. If you've been working from older figures of 8.75% and 33.75%, they're a year out of date.

Salary or dividends?

Most director-shareholders take a small salary and the rest as dividends. Salary is a business expense, so it saves Corporation Tax, but it can attract National Insurance. Dividends come out of profits that have already been taxed, but there's no National Insurance on them and the rates are lower than income tax.

The question is usually where to set the salary. With employer National Insurance starting at £5,000 but the personal allowance at £12,570, it's a real decision rather than a formality.

The Employment Allowance matters here. If you're the only director and the only employee paid above £5,000, your company can't claim it. If you have other staff, it can, and that usually makes a higher salary more attractive.

A worked example

This is a simplified example, not anyone's real figures. It assumes one director with no other income, a company profit of £50,000 before the director's pay, no Employment Allowance, and all remaining profit paid out as dividends.

Salary £5,000Salary £12,570
Employer National Insurance£0£1,135.50
Corporation Tax at 19%£8,550£6,896
Dividends paid£36,450£29,399
Dividend tax£3,051£3,107
Take-home£38,399£38,862

In this example, the £12,570 salary leaves you about £460 better off, because the Corporation Tax saving outweighs the employer National Insurance. Change the assumptions, such as other income, a different profit level or the Employment Allowance, and the answer can change. That's why it's worth running your own numbers.

Both salaries are above the lower earnings limit of £6,708, so either one keeps your National Insurance record building towards your State Pension without you paying employee National Insurance.

Use your basic-rate band

Dividends are taxed at 10.75% until your total income reaches £50,270, then at 35.75%. That jump is the main reason to plan.

If your salary and dividends so far this year leave room below £50,270, and the company has the profits, an extra dividend before 5 April 2027 uses up that cheaper band. If you're already over it, think about whether you need the money personally this year, or whether it can wait, or go into a pension instead.

Timing your dividends

When a dividend counts for tax depends on the type:

  • Interim dividends (the kind most small companies pay) count when they're actually paid.
  • Final dividends count when they're declared, unless the resolution sets a later payment date.

So a dividend paid on 4 April 2027 falls in 2026/27, and one paid on 6 April 2027 falls in 2027/28. That one-day difference can move income into a year where you have more basic-rate band to spare.

Two rules to keep you safe. Your company can only pay dividends out of available profits from this year and previous years. And each dividend needs a board minute and a dividend voucher, even if you're the only director. GOV.UK covers the basics on taking money out of a limited company.

Employer pension contributions

A pension contribution paid by your company is one of the most efficient ways to take profit out:

  • it's normally a deductible expense for Corporation Tax, as long as your overall pay package is reasonable for the work you do
  • there's no income tax or National Insurance on it for you
  • it doesn't count as your income, so it doesn't eat into your basic-rate band or push you towards £100,000

The annual allowance for 2026/27 is £60,000, including what your company pays in, and you may be able to carry forward unused allowance from the previous three tax years. The relief is given in the company accounting period in which the contribution is actually paid, so make sure the money leaves the company's account before its year end.

We've written more on business pensions for directors.

The £100,000 trap

Once your adjusted net income goes over £100,000, your personal allowance goes down by £1 for every £2 above it. By £125,140, it's gone completely. In that band, you're effectively paying tax on the income itself and on the allowance you've lost.

As a director, you can often control how much income you take. Taking less in dividends this year, making an employer pension contribution instead, or spreading dividends across two tax years can keep you below £100,000. Our post on income over £100K has more.

Shares for your spouse or civil partner

If your spouse or civil partner owns shares, dividends paid to them use their own allowances and tax bands. That can lower the family's total tax.

But HMRC can use the settlements rules to tax those dividends as yours. That risk is higher if:

  • the shares only carry a right to income, with no capital or voting rights
  • one of you waives a dividend so the other gets more
  • the gift comes with strings, such as a right to take the shares back

A genuine, outright gift of ordinary shares with full rights is usually fine, as HMRC's own settlements guidance explains. Your spouse really does own them, though, so think about it carefully and set it up properly.

An electric car through the company

A new zero-emission car bought by your company qualifies for a 100% first-year allowance, so the full cost comes off your profits in the year you buy it. For companies, that allowance ends on 31 March 2027 [CONFIRM: no further extension in the Budget 2026 documents]. After that, cars go into the main pool, and the writing-down allowance falls from 14% to 12%.

The benefit-in-kind rate for a zero-emission company car is 4% in 2026/27, rising to 5% in 2027/28. Don't buy a car for the tax break alone, but if one was already on your list, the timing matters. Talk to us before you sign anything.

Small perks that are tax-free

Trivial benefits. Your company can give a gift costing £50 or less without any tax or National Insurance, as long as it isn't cash or a cash voucher, isn't a reward for work and isn't in your contract. As a director of a close company, you're capped at £300 of trivial benefits a tax year. See GOV.UK's trivial benefits rules.

The annual party. An annual event open to all your employees is tax-free if it costs £150 a head or less, including VAT. It's not an allowance, so go over £150 and the whole amount becomes taxable.

Your checklist before 5 April 2027

  • Check your salary and dividends so far for 2026/27, and what's left of your basic-rate band.
  • Check the company has enough available profits for any further dividends, and write up the minutes and vouchers.
  • Work out whether you're heading over £100,000, and what would bring you back under.
  • Decide on an employer pension contribution, and pay it before the company's year end.
  • Thinking about an electric car? Make sure the company has actually bought it by 31 March 2027, not just ordered it, if the 100% allowance matters to you.
  • Review who owns the shares and whether that still makes sense.
  • Plan your 2027/28 salary for payroll from 6 April 2027.

Questions people ask

What's the most tax-efficient salary for a director in 2026/27?

For many single-director companies with no other staff, a salary of £12,570 works out slightly better than £5,000, because the Corporation Tax saving beats the employer National Insurance. If your company can claim the Employment Allowance, or you have other income, the answer can be different.

What are the dividend tax rates for 2026/27?

10.75% in the basic rate band, 35.75% in the higher rate band and 39.35% in the additional rate band, after a £500 dividend allowance. The Budget kept them the same for 2027/28.

Is it better to pay a dividend before or after 5 April?

It depends on how much of your basic-rate band you've used and whether you're near £100,000. An interim dividend counts in the tax year it's paid, so the date you pay it decides which year it falls in.

Can my company pay into my pension instead of paying me a dividend?

Yes. An employer contribution is normally deductible for Corporation Tax and isn't taxed on you, within your annual allowance of £60,000 plus any carry forward.
